title: Bullet holes on returning warplanes showed where armour wasn’t needed
body: Survivorship bias is the error of drawing conclusions only from the cases that made it through some filter, while the failures quietly drop out of view. We study successful companies, buildings that are still standing and investors who got rich, but rarely the ones that failed. That makes success look more predictable, and the traits of winners more special, than they really are.

slides.heading: The puzzle
slides.text: In World War II, analysts could only examine the bombers that made it home. Damage from enemy fire was spread unevenly across different parts of the planes.

slides.heading: Wald’s insight
slides.text: Statistician Abraham Wald worked on estimating vulnerability from survivors’ damage. The key idea: planes hit in the spots where survivors lacked holes didn’t come back.

steps.label: Bombers come home riddled with bullet holes
The holes cluster in some areas, not others
Planes hit in the clean spots never returned
So armour the places without holes

slides.heading: Everyday versions
slides.text: ‘They don’t make them like they used to’ forgets that the flimsy old products broke and were thrown away. Only the sturdy survivors are left to admire.

slides.question: Why do old products seem sturdier than new ones?
options: Only the sturdy old ones survived
Old owners took better care of them
slides.explanation: Survivorship bias: the flimsy old products broke and were thrown away, so only the sturdy survivors are left to admire. The failures quietly drop out of view.
